p1.key: First IE decreases down a group (outer electron further from the nucleus, more shielding) and increases across a period. Na is below Li and to the left of Mg and Al, so Na has the lowest.
MgCl2 is ionic with a high melting point (714 °C); AlCl3 sublimes at about 180 °C and behaves as a covalent (molecular) chloride, as do SiCl4, PCl3 and S2Cl2. The change comes between Mg and Al.
p1.flag: period 3 chlorides not explicitly in 2025 guide

p1.key: The last electrons go into the 4d sublevel (4d65s2, ruthenium), so the element is in the d block (group 8, not group 6).

The pattern (a dip, rises, then a large drop to 418) matches P, S, Cl, Ar, K. So N is argon, a non-metal. K and L are in the same energy level, M (Cl) is a non-metal, and P (Ca) has a higher IE than K.
Down group 1 the atoms get bigger, so metallic bonding becomes weaker and the melting point decreases. Atomic radius and reactivity increase, and electronegativity decreases.
A halogen displaces the ions of a less reactive halogen below it. Br2 is a stronger oxidizing agent than I2, so it oxidizes I− (I), but it cannot oxidize Cl− because Cl2 is more reactive: I only.

Zn<sup>2+</sup> is 3d<sup>10</sup>. With a full d sublevel no d–d transitions are possible, so its complexes are colourless. The Cr<sup>3+</sup>, Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Cu<sup>2+</sup> complexes have partly filled d sublevels and are coloured.
4s23d3 is vanadium. The 4s and 3d electrons are close in energy, so it shows variable oxidation states from +2 up to +5 (all five 4s + 3d electrons lost): +2, +3, +4, +5.
Down group 1 each atom has an extra occupied shell, so the atomic radius increases. Electronegativity, ionization energy and melting point all decrease from Li to Cs.
NaCl is ionic and dissolves without reacting, giving a neutral solution. Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub> and PCl<sub>3</sub> react with water (hydrolysis) to give acidic solutions containing HCl.

[Ar]3d<sup>2</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> (titanium) has two unpaired 3d electrons and can lose its two 4s electrons to form X<sup>2+</sup> in XCl<sub>2</sub>. [Ne]3s<sup>2</sup> has no unpaired electrons, and C and D are non-metals that would not form ionic chlorides.

First IE increases across a period as nuclear charge increases, so O < F. Mg<sup>2+</sup> is smaller than Mg, I<sub>2</sub> melts higher than Br<sub>2</sub>, and HBr is more polar than HI, so B, C and D are in decreasing order.

Non-metal oxides such as CO<sub>2</sub>, SO<sub>2</sub> and P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> are covalent (molecular) and react with water to form acidic solutions. Metal oxides tend to be ionic and basic.

Sc<sup>3+</sup> is [Ar]3d<sup>0</sup>. With no d electrons, no d–d transitions are possible, so it is colourless. Ni<sup>2+</sup>, Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Cr<sup>3+</sup> have partly filled d sublevels and are coloured.

Across period 3 the nuclear charge (number of protons) increases while the shielding from the inner shells stays about the same. The outer electrons are therefore held more tightly. The number of outer electrons does not by itself raise IE.
A ligand must donate a lone pair to the metal ion. Cl<sup>−</sup>, NCl<sub>3</sub> and PCl<sub>3</sub> each have a lone pair on the donor atom, but PCl<sub>5</sub> has no lone pair on P.

Same nuclear charge: removing an electron reduces repulsion so Br<sup>+</sup> is smallest; adding an electron increases repulsion so Br<sup>−</sup> is largest. Order: Br<sup>+</sup> < Br < Br<sup>−</sup>.
Metal oxides are basic: Na<sub>2</sub>O + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2NaOH. Non-metal oxides are acidic: SO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>. So basic, then acidic.
Across period 3, nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar, so Si is larger than Cl. In the other pairs the first species is smaller (Cl < Cl<sup>−</sup>, Na<sup>+</sup> < Na, Na < K).
Across period 3 the oxides change from ionic, basic Na<sub>2</sub>O and MgO to covalent, acidic oxides such as SO<sub>3</sub> and Cl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, which form acidic solutions.
Halogen reactivity (oxidizing strength) decreases down group 17: Cl<sub>2</sub> > Br<sub>2</sub> > I<sub>2</sub>. A halogen displaces any halide below it, so both reactions occur.

A halogen displaces a less reactive halogen (lower in the group) from its halide. Cl<sub>2</sub> is more reactive than I<sub>2</sub>, so Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2I<sup>−</sup> → 2Cl<sup>−</sup> + I<sub>2</sub> occurs; the others are the wrong way round.
2.8.8.2 is calcium (Z = 20): group 2, period 4, 40 − 20 = 20 neutrons. It forms Ca<sup>2+</sup>, so the oxide is EO, not EO<sub>2</sub>; D is the incorrect statement.
All four ions are isoelectronic (10 electrons). Radius decreases as nuclear charge increases: O<sup>2−</sup> (8 protons) > F<sup>−</sup> (9) > Na<sup>+</sup> (11) > Mg<sup>2+</sup> (12).

NH<sub>3</sub> is neutral and Cl<sup>−</sup> is −1; Pt is +2 in each. I: [Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (2 Cl<sup>−</sup> outside); II: [Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>Cl]<sup>+</sup>; III: [Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>] is neutral.

Group 1 reactivity increases down the group (K > Li, since K loses its outer electron more easily), and group 17 reactivity decreases down the group (Cl<sub>2</sub> > Br<sub>2</sub>). So K + Cl<sub>2</sub> is most vigorous.

p1.key: Across period 3, nuclear charge increases with similar shielding, so electronegativity increases and atomic radius decreases.

p1.key: From Na2O to Cl2O, bonding changes from ionic to covalent, so molten conductivity falls, and the oxides change from basic to acidic. Acid character increases, so I is wrong.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: Down both groups ionization energy falls as the outer electron is further from the nucleus. Atomic radius increases in both; melting point falls for alkali metals but rises for halogens (stronger London forces).
SO<sub>2</sub> is a small simple molecule and a gas. SiO<sub>2</sub> is a giant covalent solid and P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> is a molecular solid (m.p. about 24 °C) at room temperature.

A halogen oxidizes the halide ions of halogens below it. Br<sub>2</sub> is a stronger oxidizing agent than I<sub>2</sub>, so reaction I occurs, but weaker than Cl<sub>2</sub>, so it cannot oxidize Cl<sup>−</sup>.
Down group 1 melting points fall (weaker metallic bonding) and reactivity rises (outer electron lost more easily), so rubidium has a low melting point and reacts vigorously with water.
K<sup>+</sup>, Ar and Cl<sup>−</sup> are isoelectronic (18 electrons). Radius decreases as nuclear charge increases: K<sup>+</sup> (19 protons) is smallest, Cl<sup>−</sup> (17) is largest.
Each CN− is −1, so six contribute −6. For [Fe(CN)6]4−: Fe = −4 + 6 = +2; for [Fe(CN)6]3−: Fe = −3 + 6 = +3.

Atomic number rises by one from Li to Ne, so the number of electrons (equal to protons) increases by exactly one each time. Neutrons and atomic mass do not rise in equal steps, and all are period 2 (two occupied levels).
Halogen reactivity decreases down the group (Cl > I) while alkali metal reactivity increases (K > Li). The most reactive pair is chlorine and potassium.

A ligand forms a coordination bond by donating a lone pair to a metal ion, so it must have a non-bonding electron pair. Ligands can be neutral (H<sub>2</sub>O, NH<sub>3</sub>), so a negative charge is not essential.
A ligand needs a lone pair to donate to a metal ion. Cl<sup>−</sup>, NH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O all have lone pairs, so all three can act as ligands.
Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, so metals (on the left and lower down) have lower values than non-metals. Noble gases are usually not assigned values.
Chlorine displaces iodine from iodide; the iodine formed is coloured (brown in solution, grey-black solid). LiOH, NaCl and AgCl are colourless or white.
Na<sub>2</sub>O is a basic metal oxide: Na<sub>2</sub>O + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2NaOH, pH > 7. SiCl<sub>4</sub> hydrolyses to give HCl (acidic), NaCl is neutral and SiO<sub>2</sub> is insoluble.
Transition (d-block) elements form complex ions and act as catalysts (variable oxidation states). Their compounds are typically coloured, not colourless, so III is wrong.

Chlorine is a stronger oxidizing agent than iodine, so Cl2 oxidizes I⁻ to I2. Fluorine (not chlorine) is the strongest oxidizer, bromine cannot oxidize Cl⁻, and iodide is the strongest reducing halide.

Metallic bonding weakens down group 1 (I correct); London forces strengthen down group 17 (II correct). Across period 3 the melting point rises to a maximum at Si (covalent network) and then falls, so III is wrong.
In [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4: SO4²⁻ outside means the complex is 2+, so Co + 0 − 1 = +2 → Co = +3. In [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br: complex is 1+, Co − 2 = +1 → Co = +3. Both +3.
Atomic radius decreases across a period (Na > Mg, greater nuclear charge, same shell) and increases down a group (K > Na, extra shell). Smallest first: Mg, Na, K.
A transition element has an incomplete d sublevel in the atom or a common ion. Cr ([Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹) is a transition metal; Ca is s-block, Ge and Se are p-block.

P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> are non-metal oxides that react with water to give acids (H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>). SiO<sub>2</sub> is an acidic oxide but is insoluble in water, so it does not produce an acidic solution.
Down group 1 the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so ionization energy and electronegativity decrease. Atomic radius increases.
Adding an electron increases electron–electron repulsion with the same nuclear charge, so Cl⁻ is larger than Cl. Removing electrons makes ions smaller, so H⁺ < H⁻, Na⁺ < Na and Mg²⁺ < Mg⁺.

Across period 3, chlorides change from ionic (NaCl, MgCl<sub>2</sub>) to covalent molecular (PCl<sub>3</sub>, SCl<sub>2</sub>) as electronegativity difference falls. Oxides become more acidic, electronegativity increases and conductivity drops after Al.
p1.flag: Period 3 chlorides are not explicitly in the 2025 guide.

p1.key: Atomic and ionic radii both increase down groups 1 and 17 (extra electron shells). Boiling points decrease down group 1 (weaker metallic bonding) but increase down group 17 (stronger London forces).
Amphoteric means reacting as both an acid (with strong alkalis) and a base (with strong acids). Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is insoluble in water, so III is wrong and not evidence of amphoterism.
Cr in Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>²⁻: 2Cr − 14 = −2 → +6 (common). Fe in FeCl<sub>3</sub>: +3 (common). Mn in MnO<sub>4</sub>³⁻: Mn − 8 = −3 → +5, which is not a common oxidation state of Mn.

Non-metal chlorides (e.g. SiCl<sub>4</sub>, PCl<sub>5</sub>) hydrolyse in water to give HCl, forming acidic solutions. NaCl is neutral, molten Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub> is covalent and barely conducts, and SiCl<sub>4</sub> is a simple molecule.
p1.flag: Period 3 chlorides are not in the 2025 guide.

p1.key: The modern periodic table is arranged by atomic number, i.e. the number of protons = nuclear charge. Ordering by relative atomic mass (A) gives anomalies such as Ar/K and Te/I.

The property falls steadily from F to I. Electronegativity decreases down group 17 as atomic radius increases and shielding increases. Atomic radius, density and melting point all increase down the group.
NaCl is an ionic chloride that simply dissolves to give a neutral solution (pH 7). AlCl3, PCl3 and Cl2 all react with water to give acidic solutions (e.g. PCl3 forms HCl). A.
p1.flag: reactions of period 3 chlorides with water not in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2: hydrogen gas is evolved, the reaction is exothermic, and NaOH dissolves to give a clear, colourless solution. All three are true. D.
The K atom has four occupied shells, the most of all four species. K+ and Cl− have only three shells, and Na+ has two. So K is largest.

In a complex, ligands split the d orbitals into two energy levels. Visible light is absorbed as an electron moves from a lower to a higher d orbital, and we see the complementary colour. It is absorption, not emission, and d–d, not s–d.

Elements in the same group (not period) have similar chemical properties, so I is false. Group 17 shows a gradual change in physical properties (II), and across period 3 the number of outer (valence) electrons increases with position (III). C.
Across period 3 the oxides change from ionic (Na2O, MgO) to covalent (P4O10, SO3) and from basic to acidic. First IE increases generally but not linearly: there are dips at Al and S. A.
In [CuCl4]2−: Cu + 4(−1) = −2, so Cu is +2 (I). Four Cl− ions each donate a lone pair to Cu, so they are ligands (III) and the coordination number is 4 (II). D.
Br− has four occupied shells, more than Cl− and K+ (three each) and F− (two), so it is the largest. K+ is smaller than Cl− because it has a greater nuclear charge for the same configuration.
Non-metal oxides are acidic: P4O10 gives H3PO4 and SO3 gives H2SO4. MgO is a basic metal oxide, forming Mg(OH)2. B: I and III only.
Ligands donate lone pairs to the central metal ion. In [Fe(CN)6]3−, the six CN− ions are the ligands around Fe3+. K+ is just the counter-ion.

Mg, Ca and Sr are all group 2, so they have similar chemical properties (I). Elements in the same period have the same number of occupied main energy levels (II). P4O10 is an acidic oxide, so III is false. A.
I: water is neutral, so Fe = +3. II: one CN− and overall 2+: Fe − 1 = +2, so Fe = +3. III: 6 CN− and overall 3−: Fe − 6 = −3, so Fe = +3. All three. D.

Across period 3 nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same, so electrons are pulled closer and atomic radius decreases. Atomic number, electronegativity and (generally) first IE increase.

Oxidizing power of the halogens decreases down the group, so Cl<sub>2</sub> oxidizes I⁻ to I<sub>2</sub> (Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I<sub>2</sub>). Br<sub>2</sub> cannot oxidize Cl⁻, and F<sub>2</sub> is the most easily reduced, strongest oxidant.
Ligands split the d orbitals into two energy levels; absorbing visible light promotes an electron from a lower to a higher d orbital (a d–d transition). The complementary colour is seen.
Electronegativity decreases down group 17, so F is the most electronegative halogen. Cs (very low electronegativity) and F give the largest difference.
A ligand must have a lone pair to donate to the metal ion. Cl⁻, NH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O all have lone pairs, so all three can act as ligands.

Colour needs a partly filled d sublevel. Ni<sup>2+</sup> is 3d<sup>8</sup>, so its solution is green. Zn<sup>2+</sup> (3d<sup>10</sup>), Sc<sup>3+</sup> (3d<sup>0</sup>) and Mg<sup>2+</sup> (no d electrons) are colourless.

The graph peaks at the group 1 metals (Li, Na, K) and falls across each period, which is the pattern for atomic radius. First IE and electronegativity show the opposite trend (lowest at group 1). Noble gases are omitted, as is usual for atomic radius data.

A halogen oxidizes the halide ions of halogens below it. Cl<sub>2</sub> and Br<sub>2</sub> both oxidize I⁻ (I and II occur), but I<sub>2</sub> is a weaker oxidant than Br<sub>2</sub> and cannot oxidize Br⁻ (III does not occur).

A transition element has an incomplete d sublevel in the atom or one of its common ions. Ti and Fe qualify. Zn (and Zn<sup>2+</sup>) has a full 3d<sup>10</sup> sublevel, so it is not a transition element.
K⁺, Cl⁻ and S<sup>2−</sup> are isoelectronic (18 electrons). Radius decreases as nuclear charge increases: K⁺ (19 protons) < Cl⁻ (17) < S<sup>2−</sup> (16).
Metal oxides (Na<sub>2</sub>O, MgO) are basic; non-metal oxides (SiO<sub>2</sub>, chlorine oxides) are acidic. So chlorine acidic, magnesium basic, silicon acidic, sodium basic.
F⁻, Na⁺, Mg<sup>2+</sup> and Al<sup>3+</sup> are isoelectronic (10 electrons). Radius decreases as the number of protons increases (9 → 13): F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg<sup>2+</sup> > Al<sup>3+</sup>.

Zn<sup>2+</sup> has a full 3d<sup>10</sup> sublevel, so no d–d transitions are possible and the complex is colourless. Fe<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>), Ni<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>) and Co<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>) complexes are coloured.
The first electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one gaseous atom gains one electron to form a gaseous 1− ion: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g).

Down group 1 an extra shell is added, so atomic radius increases. The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so first IE decreases, and weaker metallic bonding lowers the melting point.

A halogen displaces a less reactive halide ion. Cl<sub>2</sub> is a stronger oxidizing agent than Br<sub>2</sub>, so it oxidizes Br<sup>−</sup> to Br<sub>2</sub>. I<sub>2</sub> cannot oxidize Br<sup>−</sup> or Cl<sup>−</sup>, and F<sub>2</sub> cannot be formed from F<sup>−</sup> by Cl<sub>2</sub>.

All three oxides are solids at room temperature. Na<sub>2</sub>O and Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> are ionic, so their ions are mobile when molten and they conduct. P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> is a covalent molecular solid with no ions, so it conducts poorly.

Across a period the nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same, so atoms attract bonding electrons more strongly and electronegativity increases. Electronegativity decreases down a group, non-metals have higher values than metals, and noble gases are usually not assigned values.

A halogen oxidizes the halide ions of halogens below it. F<sub>2</sub> displaces Cl<sup>−</sup>, giving Cl<sub>2</sub>, and Br<sub>2</sub> displaces I<sup>−</sup>, giving I<sub>2</sub>. I<sub>2</sub> is a weaker oxidizing agent than Cl<sub>2</sub>, so II does not happen.

Oxides become more acidic across period 3 as the element's oxidation state and electronegativity rise. Cl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (Cl +7) forms the very strong acid HClO<sub>4</sub>. SiO<sub>2</sub> is insoluble and only weakly acidic.

Group 5 (now group 15), period 4 is arsenic, [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>4p<sup>3</sup>. It has 4 occupied energy levels and 5 valence electrons, and it is a p-block element, not a transition element. It can gain 3 electrons to form X<sup>3−</sup>.

Down group 1 the atomic and ionic radii increase and the first IE decreases, because the outer electron is further from the nucleus. Melting point decreases because the metallic bonding gets weaker, so I is wrong.

Al<sup>3+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup> and Na<sup>+</sup> are isoelectronic (10 electrons). As nuclear charge rises (11 → 13) the electrons are pulled in more, so the radius order is Al<sup>3+</sup> < Mg<sup>2+</sup> < Na<sup>+</sup>. In A, Cl<sup>−</sup> is larger than Cl. B and D are in decreasing order.

Non-metal oxides such as P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> and SO<sub>3</sub> react with water to form acids (H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>). Na<sub>2</sub>O and MgO are basic. Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is amphoteric and SiO<sub>2</sub> is insoluble, so neither gives an acidic solution.

Zn<sup>2+</sup> has a full 3d<sup>10</sup> sublevel, so no d–d electron transitions are possible and its compounds are colourless. The Fe<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>), Co<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>) and Ni<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>) complexes all have partly filled d orbitals and are coloured.

Na<sup>+</sup> > Mg<sup>2+</sup> > Al<sup>3+</sup> decrease in size (isoelectronic, rising nuclear charge). The anions P<sup>3−</sup>, S<sup>2−</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> have an extra electron shell, so they are much larger and also decrease across. This matches the chart.

Reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group, so K is more vigorous than Na (I true) and K more vigorous than Li (II false). Halogen reactivity decreases down the group, so F<sub>2</sub> reacts more vigorously than Br<sub>2</sub> with I<sup>−</sup> (III true).

Sc<sup>3+</sup> has the configuration [Ar]3d<sup>0</sup>. With no d electrons, no d–d transitions are possible, so the ion is colourless. Cr<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>3</sup>) and Fe<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup>) complexes are coloured.

Across period 3 the oxides change from basic (Na<sub>2</sub>O) to acidic (Cl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) and the bonding changes from ionic to covalent, so I and II are correct. III is false: e.g. SiO<sub>2</sub> and Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> are insoluble in water.
Potassium starts a new shell (4s1) so has the lowest IE; Ca has a higher nuclear charge in the same shell; argon, a noble gas with a full outer shell, is highest: K < Ca < Ar.

The Co ion accepts lone pairs from the ligands, so it is a Lewis acid (I). Charge: x + 5(0) + (−1) = +2, so Co is +3, not +2 (II false). Six ligands give an octahedral complex with 90° bond angles (III).

The sudden drop from 2081 to 496 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> marks a new period: 496 and 738 are a group 1 and group 2 element (Na, Mg). 1314, 1681 and 2081 rise to a noble gas (O, F, Ne), so these are the last three of one period and the first two of the next.
[Cu(NH3)2Cl2] is neutral: x + 0 + 2(−1) = 0, so Cu is +2 (I). NH3 donates a lone pair, so it is a ligand (II). Cl− ions also donate electron pairs, so they act as Lewis bases, not acids (III wrong).
Na2O is formed from a metal and a non-metal with a large electronegativity difference, so it is ionic. It reacts with water to form NaOH, so it is basic.
Electronegativity is a relative measure (no units) of the ability of a bonded atom to attract a shared pair of electrons. B is ionization energy, C is electron affinity, and D wrongly gives it units.

A ligand must donate a lone pair. NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> has no lone pair on N (all four pairs are bonded to H), so it cannot be a ligand. H<sub>2</sub>O, Cl<sup>−</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup> all have lone pairs.

IE increases across a period and decreases down a group. Argon, a noble gas at the end of period 3, has the highest nuclear charge in that period and a stable full outer shell, so it has the greatest first IE. Cs has the lowest.
As, Bi, P and Sb are all in group 15. A mixes groups 1 and 2; B lists period 3 elements; C mixes transition metals with Pb (group 14).

Transition metals can change oxidation number easily, so they can gain and lose electrons during a reaction (and can adsorb reactants via d orbitals), allowing them to act as catalysts. Split d sub-levels explain colour, not catalysis.
Six CN− ligands around Fe3+ give six electron domains around the central ion, so the complex is octahedral (bond angles 90°).
The drop after C matches the group 15 → 16 dip (pairing of electrons in a p orbital), so C is group 15 and B is group 14. A is group 13 and D is group 16.
Arsenic lies on the metal/non-metal staircase, with intermediate properties, so it is a metalloid. Co is a transition metal, Cs an alkali metal and Es an actinide.

Electronegativity decreases down a group (more shielding, larger radius) and increases across a period (greater nuclear charge). Atomic radius decreases across a period; IE decreases down but increases across.

Colour depends on the d-orbital splitting, which is affected by the metal's oxidation state, the identity of the ligands and the number/geometry of ligands. The isotope has the same electron arrangement, so it has no effect.

Ligands split the d orbitals; d electrons absorb visible light of a particular frequency as they are promoted to the higher set. We see the complementary colour of the light absorbed. It is absorption, not emission.

Down group 17 the molecules get larger with more electrons, so London forces strengthen and boiling point increases. Electron affinity, first ionization energy and reactivity all generally decrease down the group.
2K + 2H2O → 2KOH + H2. The reaction is exothermic and the final products are potassium hydroxide and hydrogen; the solution is alkaline (pH > 7), not neutral.
Co3+ + 5 neutral NH3 + Br− gives an overall charge of 2+ (I), and six ligands make it octahedral (II). Co3+ is [Ar]3d6, which is not half-filled, so III is false.

Ligands split the Cu2+ d orbitals; a d electron absorbs visible light to jump to a higher-energy d orbital, and the complementary colour (blue) is seen. Colour is not due to light emitted, nor to ligand–metal or d–s transitions.

In S (3p4) one 3p orbital holds a pair of electrons; repulsion between the paired electrons makes one easier to remove than the unpaired 3p electrons of P (3p3), so IE drops from P to S. The Mg → Al drop is due to the higher-energy 3p sublevel, not a lower one.
S2− and Cl− have three shells; Mg2+ and Al3+ have two. In each isoelectronic pair, more protons pull electrons in more tightly: S2− > Cl− > Mg2+ > Al3+.
Na2O is a strongly basic oxide that reacts with water to form NaOH, a soluble strong base: highest pH. MgO is only slightly soluble (weakly alkaline); SO3 and CO2 are acidic oxides.
Fe3+ + 2 OH− + 4 neutral H2O = (+3) + 2(−1) + 0 = 1+. This is consistent with one Br− counter-ion making the compound neutral.
Ne (noble gas, full shell) has the highest first IE, 2081 = X; Na has the lowest, 496 = Y; Mg is 738 = Z. Atomic numbers Ne 10, Na 11, Mg 12, so X < Y < Z.
Each element down Group 1 has an extra electron shell, so atomic radius increases. Electronegativity, first ionization energy and melting point all decrease down the group.
The lanthanides are the f-block elements La–Lu (Z = 57–71); terbium (Tb, Z = 65) is one of them. U is an actinide, while Hf and Y are d-block transition metals.

NH3 molecules replace H2O ligands, forming deep blue [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+. The d orbitals are already split in the aqua complex; the stronger ligand makes the splitting larger, and the colour deepens rather than fades.

Across period 3, increasing nuclear charge makes atomic radius decrease and first IE generally increase. Melting point rises to a maximum at Si and then falls sharply for the molecular non-metals, so II is false.
P4O10 is a non-metal oxide; it reacts with water to give phosphoric acid (P4O10 + 6H2O → 4H3PO4), pH < 7. MgO, Li2O and CaO are basic oxides giving alkaline solutions.

Both contain Co3+. Different ligands split the 3d orbitals by different amounts, so different wavelengths are absorbed and different colours seen. An orange complex absorbs the complementary colour (blue), not orange.

Down group 1 the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so first IE decreases. Atomic radius increases down group 17 and decreases across period 3; first IE generally increases across period 3.

The colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed. An orange complex absorbs blue light, the highest-energy light among these (green absorbs red, blue absorbs orange, violet absorbs yellow), so [Fe(H2O)6]3+ has the largest splitting.

Across a period nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same, so electrons are held more tightly: first ionization energy and electronegativity both increase. Atomic radius decreases across a period, ruling out B and C.
Lead (Pb) is in group 14, so its outer electrons are in a 6p sublevel: p-block. Pm and Pu are f-block (lanthanide/actinide) and Pt is a d-block transition metal.

Ligands further right in the spectrochemical series cause a larger splitting of the d orbitals. H2O is to the right of Cl−, so it increases the d–d separation more. The splitting is between d orbitals, not p and d, and the series alone cannot predict a specific colour.

Non-metal oxides are acidic: P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub>/P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> form phosphorus oxoacids, NO<sub>2</sub> forms HNO<sub>2</sub>/HNO<sub>3</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> forms H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>. Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is amphoteric and insoluble, and SiO<sub>2</sub> does not dissolve in water, so I is wrong.
The sulfate (2−) balances the complex, so the complex ion is [Fe(H2O)5Cl]2+. H2O is neutral and Cl− is −1, so Fe + (−1) = +2, giving Fe = +3.
Bi is in period 6, so its outer electrons are in n = 6. It is in group 15 (6s26p3), so it has 5 valence electrons. "15" is the group number, not the number of valence electrons.
Mg is in period 3 (an extra shell), so it is largest. Across period 2, radius decreases as nuclear charge rises: Be > C > N. Order: Mg > Be > C > N.

Ligands split the d orbitals. The complex absorbs visible light of a frequency matching the gap as a d electron is promoted to a higher d orbital; the colour seen is the complementary colour of the light that is transmitted. Colour does not come from emission.

Down group 17 the atoms gain extra electron shells, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded. Ionization energy decreases and the ionic radius increases (F− < Cl− < Br− < I−).
One Cl− is outside the brackets, so the complex is [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+. NH3 is neutral and two Cl− give −2, so Co − 2 = +1 and Co = +3.
Even unpolluted rain dissolves atmospheric CO2, forming the weak acid H2CO3, so its pH is about 5.6. SO2 and nitrogen oxides cause acid rain (pollution), and methane is not acidic.

Across period 2 nuclear charge rises with similar shielding, so electronegativity increases steadily from Li to F. Melting point and conductivity peak in the middle (carbon/metals), and ionic radius does not rise steadily.
Samarium (Sm) is a lanthanide, so its highest-energy electrons are in 4f: f-block. Sc is d-block, Sn is p-block and Sr is s-block.
A stronger-field ligand causes a larger d–d splitting, so the light absorbed has higher energy and therefore a shorter wavelength (E = hc/λ).
Down group 1 each element has an extra occupied shell, so atomic radius increases. Electronegativity, first ionization energy and melting point all decrease down the group.
Cobalt (Z = 27) is in the d-block ([Ar]3d<sup>7</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>). Ca is s-block, Cl is p-block and Cf is f-block.
Colour depends on the size of the d-orbital splitting, which is set by the metal, its oxidation state and the ligand. Temperature does not change it.

Electron affinity is the energy change when one mole of gaseous atoms gains one mole of electrons: X(g) + e<sup>−</sup> → X<sup>−</sup>(g). Option A is an ionization energy and C is bond breaking (atomization).

SO<sub>2</sub> (from burning sulfur-containing fuels) dissolves in rain to form sulfurous/sulfuric acid. CO<sub>2</sub> only makes rain weakly acidic (pH ≈ 5.6), not acid deposition; SiO<sub>2</sub> is insoluble and SrO is basic.
IE generally increases across period 3, but Al is lower than Mg because its outermost electron is in a 3p sublevel, higher in energy and more shielded than Mg's 3s. Order: Na < Al < Mg.
Reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group (outer electron lost more easily), so caesium is most reactive; halogen reactivity decreases down the group, so fluorine is most reactive.

Paramagnetic ions have unpaired electrons. Ti<sup>3+</sup> is 3d<sup>1</sup>, Cr<sup>3+</sup> is 3d<sup>3</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> is 3d<sup>5</sup>: all have unpaired electrons, so all three are paramagnetic.

Violet [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> absorbs the complementary colour, yellow (λ ≈ 5.8 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m). Yellow [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> absorbs violet, shorter λ and higher energy, so NH<sub>3</sub> causes larger splitting: H<sub>2</sub>O < NH<sub>3</sub>.
Across period 3 oxides change from basic (Na<sub>2</sub>O) to amphoteric (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) to acidic (SO<sub>3</sub>).
Down group 1 atomic radius increases and reactivity with water increases (outer electron is lost more easily). Melting point decreases because metallic bonding weakens.

Both complexes have the same ligand (Cl<sup>−</sup>), the same charge on the metal (+2) and the same geometry; only the metal differs (Ni<sup>2+</sup> vs Co<sup>2+</sup>), which changes the d-electron number and splitting.
